muscles.sourceName: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Pectoral Girdle and Upper Limbs

muscles.title: Abductor digiti minimi of the hand
muscles.origin: Pisiform and tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris
muscles.insertion: Base of the proximal phalanx of the fifth digit
muscles.actions: Abducts the little finger and assists flexion at its metacarpophalangeal joint.
muscles.imageAlt: Focused Gray anatomy plate highlighting abductor digiti minimi of the hand in red
muscles.imageCredit: Henry Gray, Wikimedia Commons, public domain
muscles.sourceName: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Pectoral Girdle and Upper Limbs

muscles.title: Flexor digiti minimi brevis of the hand
muscles.origin: Hook of hamate and flexor retinaculum
muscles.insertion: Base of the proximal phalanx of the fifth digit
muscles.actions: Flexes the little finger at the metacarpophalangeal joint.
muscles.imageAlt: Focused Gray anatomy plate highlighting flexor digiti minimi brevis of the hand in red
muscles.imageCredit: Henry Gray, Wikimedia Commons, public domain
muscles.sourceName: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Pectoral Girdle and Upper Limbs

muscles.title: Opponens digiti minimi
muscles.origin: Hook of hamate and flexor retinaculum
muscles.insertion: Medial border of the fifth metacarpal
muscles.actions: Draws the fifth metacarpal forward and rotates it to cup the palm.
muscles.imageAlt: Focused Gray anatomy plate highlighting opponens digiti minimi in red
muscles.imageCredit: Henry Gray, Wikimedia Commons, public domain
muscles.sourceName: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Pectoral Girdle and Upper Limbs

muscles.title: Palmar interossei of the hand
muscles.origin: Palmar surfaces of metacarpals two, four, and five
muscles.insertion: Bases of proximal phalanges and extensor expansions of the same digits
muscles.actions: Adduct the fingers toward the middle finger and assist coordinated finger flexion and extension.
muscles.imageAlt: Focused Gray anatomy plate highlighting the palmar interossei of the hand in red
muscles.imageCredit: Henry Gray, Wikimedia Commons, public domain
muscles.sourceName: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Pectoral Girdle and Upper Limbs

muscles.title: Flexor digiti minimi brevis of the foot
muscles.origin: Base of the fifth metatarsal and sheath of fibularis longus
muscles.insertion: Base of the proximal phalanx of the fifth toe
muscles.actions: Flexes the little toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint and supports lateral-foot control.
muscles.imageAlt: Plantar Gray's Anatomy plate isolating the flexor digiti minimi brevis of the foot
muscles.imageCredit: Uwe Gille after Gray's Anatomy, Wikimedia Commons, public domain
muscles.sourceName: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Pelvic Girdle and Lower Limbs

muscles.title: Puborectalis
muscles.origin: Posterior surface of the pubic body and inferior pubic ramus
muscles.insertion: Forms a muscular sling behind the anorectal junction and joins the opposite side
muscles.actions: Maintains the anorectal angle, supports fecal continence, and relaxes during defecation.
muscles.imageAlt: OpenStax pelvic floor diagram identifying the puborectalis portion of levator ani
muscles.imageCredit: OpenStax, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0
muscles.sourceName: NCBI StatPearls, Anatomy of the Pelvic Floor

muscles.title: Pubococcygeus
muscles.origin: Posterior pubis and anterior portion of the tendinous arch of levator ani
muscles.insertion: Perineal body, anococcygeal raphe, coccyx, and connective tissue around pelvic organs
muscles.actions: Supports and elevates the pelvic viscera and contributes to urinary and fecal continence.
muscles.imageAlt: OpenStax pelvic floor diagram identifying the pubococcygeus portion of levator ani
muscles.imageCredit: OpenStax, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0
muscles.sourceName: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Axial Muscles of the Abdominal Wall and Thorax

muscles.title: Iliococcygeus
muscles.origin: Tendinous arch of levator ani and ischial spine
muscles.insertion: Anococcygeal raphe and coccyx
muscles.actions: Forms the lateral levator plate, supports pelvic organs, and elevates the pelvic floor.
muscles.imageAlt: OpenStax pelvic floor diagram identifying the iliococcygeus portion of levator ani
muscles.imageCredit: OpenStax, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0
muscles.sourceName: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Axial Muscles of the Abdominal Wall and Thorax

muscles.title: Superficial transverse perineal
muscles.origin: Ischial tuberosity and adjacent ischial ramus
muscles.insertion: Perineal body
muscles.actions: Stabilizes the perineal body and supports the central pelvic outlet.
muscles.imageAlt: OpenStax perineal diagram identifying the superficial transverse perineal muscle
muscles.imageCredit: OpenStax, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0
muscles.sourceName: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Axial Muscles of the Abdominal Wall and Thorax

muscles.title: Bulbospongiosus
muscles.origin: Perineal body and midline raphe over the bulb or vestibule
muscles.insertion: Perineal membrane and erectile tissues surrounding the bulb or vestibule
muscles.actions: Compresses erectile tissue, assists emptying of the urethra, and contributes to sexual function.
muscles.imageAlt: Focused inferior anatomical illustration isolating the female bulbospongiosus muscle
muscles.imageCredit: Uwe Gille after Gray's Anatomy, Wikimedia Commons, public domain
muscles.sourceName: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Axial Muscles of the Abdominal Wall and Thorax

muscles.title: Ischiocavernosus
muscles.origin: Ischial tuberosity and ischiopubic ramus
muscles.insertion: Crus of the penis or clitoris and its investing fascia
muscles.actions: Compresses the crus to help maintain erection by limiting venous outflow.
muscles.imageAlt: Focused inferior anatomical illustration isolating the male ischiocavernosus muscle
muscles.imageCredit: Uwe Gille after Gray's Anatomy, Wikimedia Commons, public domain
muscles.sourceName: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Axial Muscles of the Abdominal Wall and Thorax

muscles.title: External urethral sphincter
muscles.origin: Ischiopubic rami and perineal membrane
muscles.insertion: Encircles the urethra and blends with the perineal body and adjacent fibers
muscles.actions: Voluntarily compresses the urethra and contributes to urinary continence.
muscles.imageAlt: OpenStax diagram identifying the external urethral sphincter
muscles.imageCredit: OpenStax, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0
muscles.sourceName: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Axial Muscles of the Abdominal Wall and Thorax

muscles.title: External anal sphincter
muscles.origin: Perineal body and anococcygeal ligament
muscles.insertion: Encircles the anal canal and blends with surrounding perineal fibers
muscles.actions: Voluntarily closes the anal canal and supports fecal continence.
muscles.imageAlt: OpenStax diagram identifying the external anal sphincter
muscles.imageCredit: OpenStax, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0
muscles.sourceName: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Axial Muscles of the Abdominal Wall and Thorax

muscles.title: Subclavius
muscles.origin: Junction of the first rib and its costal cartilage
muscles.insertion: Inferior surface of the middle third of the clavicle
muscles.actions: Anchors and depresses the clavicle and helps steady the sternoclavicular joint.
muscles.imageAlt: Frontal 3D anatomy view with the subclavius muscle highlighted in red beneath the clavicle
muscles.imageCredit: Anatomography / DBCLS, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.1 Japan
muscles.sourceName: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Pectoral Girdle and Upper Limbs

muscles.title: Transversus thoracis
muscles.origin: Posterior surface of the lower sternum and xiphoid process
muscles.insertion: Internal surfaces of costal cartilages two through six
muscles.actions: Weakly depresses the ribs and assists forced expiration while stabilizing the anterior chest wall.
muscles.imageAlt: Gray anatomy plate depicting the transversus thoracis muscles on the inner anterior chest wall
muscles.imageCredit: Gray's Anatomy, plate 390, Wikimedia Commons, public domain
muscles.sourceName: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Axial Muscles of the Abdominal Wall and Thorax

muscles.title: Subcostals
muscles.origin: Internal surfaces of lower ribs near their angles
muscles.insertion: Internal surface of the second or third rib below
muscles.actions: Depress the ribs during forced expiration and help stabilize the posterior thoracic wall.
muscles.imageAlt: Historical anatomy plate identifying the subcostals on the internal posterior thoracic wall
muscles.imageCredit: Physiology and biochemistry in modern medicine (1918), Wikimedia Commons, public domain
muscles.sourceName: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Axial Muscles of the Abdominal Wall and Thorax

muscles.title: Serratus posterior superior
muscles.origin: Nuchal ligament and spinous processes from C7 through T3
muscles.insertion: Superior borders of ribs two through five
muscles.actions: Assists elevation and proprioceptive control of the upper ribs during breathing.
muscles.imageAlt: Posterior Anatomography rendering highlighting the serratus posterior superior muscle in red
muscles.imageCredit: Anatomography / DBCLS, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP
muscles.sourceName: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Head, Neck, and Back

muscles.title: Serratus posterior inferior
muscles.origin: Spinous processes from T11 through L2 and thoracolumbar fascia
muscles.insertion: Inferior borders of ribs nine through twelve
muscles.actions: Assists depression and proprioceptive control of the lower ribs during breathing.
muscles.imageAlt: Posterior Anatomography rendering highlighting the serratus posterior inferior muscle in red
muscles.imageCredit: Anatomography / DBCLS, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP
muscles.sourceName: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Head, Neck, and Back

muscles.title: Psoas major
muscles.origin: Bodies, discs, and transverse processes from T12 through L5
muscles.insertion: Lesser trochanter of the femur through the iliopsoas tendon
muscles.actions: Flexes the hip, assists external rotation, and can flex or laterally stabilize the trunk when the femur is fixed.
muscles.imageAlt: Anterior Anatomography model highlighting the psoas major from the lumbar spine to the proximal femur
muscles.imageCredit: BodyParts3D / Anatomography, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP
muscles.sourceName: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Pelvic Girdle and Lower Limbs

muscles.title: Iliacus
muscles.origin: Iliac fossa and inner surface of the iliac crest
muscles.insertion: Lesser trochanter of the femur through the iliopsoas tendon
muscles.actions: Flexes the hip and helps stabilize the femoral head and pelvis during gait.

muscles.title: Psoas minor
muscles.origin: Bodies of T12 and L1 and the intervening disc
muscles.insertion: Pectineal line, iliopubic eminence, and iliac fascia
muscles.actions: Weakly flexes the lumbar trunk and tensions the iliac fascia; this muscle is absent in many people.

muscles.title: Articularis genus
muscles.origin: Distal anterior surface of the femur
muscles.insertion: Suprapatellar bursa and anterior knee joint capsule

muscles.title: Extensor hallucis brevis
muscles.origin: Superolateral surface of the calcaneus
muscles.insertion: Dorsal base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe
muscles.actions: Extends the great toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint and assists controlled toe clearance.
muscles.imageAlt: Anterior three-dimensional anatomical view highlighting the extensor hallucis brevis in red
muscles.imageCredit: Was a bee / BodyParts3D, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP
muscles.sourceName: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Pelvic Girdle and Lower Limbs

muscles.title: Deep transverse perineal
muscles.origin: Medial surface of the ischial ramus and ischial tuberosity
muscles.insertion: Perineal body and fibers of the opposite side
muscles.actions: Stabilizes the perineal body and reinforces the deep perineal space; its morphology varies by sex and individual.

muscles.imageCredit: OpenStax, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0
muscles.sourceName: NCBI StatPearls, Deep Perineal Space

muscles.title: Compressor urethrae
muscles.origin: Ischiopubic ramus on each side
muscles.insertion: Joins its opposite muscle anterior to the urethra
muscles.actions: Compresses the urethra and contributes to urinary continence in female pelvic anatomy.

muscles.imageCredit: OpenStax, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0
muscles.sourceName: NCBI StatPearls, Deep Perineal Space

muscles.title: Urethrovaginal sphincter
muscles.origin: Perineal body
muscles.insertion: Loops around the distal urethra and vagina and joins fibers from the opposite side
muscles.actions: Constricts the urethral and vaginal openings and contributes to continence and pelvic support in female pelvic anatomy.
muscles.imageAlt: OpenStax perineal anatomy diagram identifying the female urethrovaginal sphincter muscle region
muscles.imageCredit: OpenStax, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0
muscles.sourceName: NCBI StatPearls, Deep Perineal Space

muscles.title: Anterior scalene
muscles.origin: Anterior tubercles of the transverse processes from C3 through C6
muscles.insertion: Scalene tubercle and superior surface of the first rib
muscles.actions: Flexes and laterally flexes the neck and elevates the first rib during deep inspiration.

muscles.title: Middle scalene
muscles.origin: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes from C2 through C7
muscles.insertion: Superior surface of the first rib posterior to the subclavian groove
muscles.actions: Laterally flexes the neck and elevates the first rib during deep inspiration.
muscles.imageAlt: Rotating Anatomography rendering highlighting the middle scalene scalenus medius muscle in red
muscles.imageCredit: Anatomography / DBCLS, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP
muscles.sourceName: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Head, Neck, and Back

muscles.title: Posterior scalene
muscles.origin: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes from C4 through C6
muscles.insertion: External surface of the second rib
muscles.actions: Laterally flexes the neck and elevates the second rib during deep inspiration.

muscles.title: Sternohyoid
muscles.origin: Posterior manubrium and medial end of the clavicle
muscles.insertion: Body of the hyoid bone
muscles.actions: Depresses the hyoid after swallowing and helps stabilize it during speech.

muscles.sourceName: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Head, Neck, and Back

muscles.title: Omohyoid
muscles.origin: Superior border of the scapula near the suprascapular notch
muscles.insertion: Inferior border of the hyoid through an intermediate tendon
muscles.actions: Depresses, retracts, and steadies the hyoid after it has been elevated.
muscles.imageAlt: Gray's Anatomy anterior neck plate highlighting both bellies of the omohyoid muscle
muscles.imageCredit: Gray's Anatomy, highlighted by Helgo13, Wikimedia Commons, public domain
muscles.sourceName: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Head, Neck, and Back

muscles.title: Sternothyroid
muscles.origin: Posterior surface of the manubrium
muscles.insertion: Oblique line of the thyroid cartilage
muscles.actions: Depresses the larynx and thyroid cartilage after swallowing and during vocal control.

muscles.sourceName: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Head, Neck, and Back

muscles.title: Thyrohyoid
muscles.origin: Oblique line of the thyroid cartilage
muscles.insertion: Inferior border of the body and greater horn of the hyoid
muscles.actions: Depresses the hyoid or elevates the larynx when the hyoid is fixed.

muscles.title: Rectus capitis posterior major
muscles.origin: Spinous process of C2
muscles.insertion: Lateral portion of the inferior nuchal line of the occipital bone

muscles.insertion: Medial portion of the inferior nuchal line of the occipital bone

muscles.title: Obliquus capitis superior
muscles.origin: Transverse process of C1
muscles.insertion: Occipital bone between the superior and inferior nuchal lines

muscles.title: Obliquus capitis inferior

muscles.insertion: Transverse process of C1

muscles.origin: Common erector-spinae tendon from the sacrum, iliac crest, and thoracolumbar fascia
muscles.insertion: Angles of the lower six ribs and upper lumbar transverse processes

muscles.insertion: Angles of ribs one through six and the transverse process of C7
muscles.actions: Extends the thoracic spine and laterally flexes it toward the working side.

muscles.title: Iliocostalis cervicis
muscles.origin: Angles of ribs three through six
muscles.insertion: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes from C4 through C6

muscles.origin: Common erector-spinae tendon, sacrum, and lumbar transverse processes

muscles.title: Spinalis thoracis

muscles.title: Rectus capitis anterior

muscles.title: Rectus capitis lateralis

muscles.title: Platysma

recipes.title: Squat preparation
recipes.goal: Prepare the hips, ankles, and trunk for a more comfortable squat pattern
recipes.whenToUse: Your squat feels restricted or uneven, but normal daily movement is otherwise comfortable.
recipes.equipment: Chair or counter, open floor space
recipes.steps:
1. Take five relaxed breaths in a supported squat or sit-to-stand position.
2. Practice controlled ankle rocks without lifting the heel.
3. Perform a slow supported squat for a comfortable range.
4. Repeat an unassisted squat only if the supported version feels steady.
recipes.dosage: Use 2 rounds of 5 ankle rocks and 5 slow squats. Keep 2–3 comfortable repetitions in reserve.
recipes.reassess: Compare depth, balance, heel contact, and comfort with your first repetition.
recipes.regression: Raise the chair height, reduce depth, or hold a stable support.
recipes.progression: Add a pause near the lowest comfortable position before standing.
recipes.cautions: Stop if pain sharpens, symptoms spread, the knee or hip gives way, or balance feels unsafe.
recipes.relatedConditions: Limited squat depth, ankle mobility, pelvic control

recipes.title: Scapular control sequence
recipes.goal: Restore comfortable scapular movement before loaded overhead work
recipes.whenToUse: Overhead reach feels stiff or the shoulder blade feels difficult to control without acute pain.
recipes.steps:
1. Set a relaxed rib position with three slow breaths.
2. Practice a gentle wall reach without shrugging.
3. Add a short-range wall slide while keeping the neck relaxed.
4. Reassess an unloaded overhead reach.
recipes.dosage: Perform 2 rounds of 5–8 controlled repetitions with a full exhale between rounds.
recipes.reassess: Check whether reach feels smoother and whether the neck stays relaxed.
recipes.regression: Use a smaller range and keep both forearms supported on the wall.
recipes.progression: Add light band resistance only after the wall version stays smooth.
recipes.cautions: Stop for sharp pain, new weakness, numbness, or symptoms traveling down the arm.
recipes.sourceName: AAOS Rotator Cuff and Shoulder Conditioning Program

recipes.title: Neck desk reset
recipes.goal: Reduce accumulated neck effort and restore comfortable head and shoulder movement
recipes.whenToUse: The neck feels tired or stiff after prolonged sitting and gentle movement usually helps.
recipes.steps:
1. Sit tall without forcing the chest upward.
2. Take three slow breaths and let the shoulders soften.
3. Perform small pain-free head turns.
4. Add a gentle wall-supported reach.
5. Recheck head turning before returning to work.
recipes.dosage: Use 3 breaths, 4–6 turns per side, and 5 controlled reaches.
recipes.reassess: Compare turning range, effort, and comfort on each side.
recipes.regression: Reduce the turning range and keep the head supported against a wall or chair.
recipes.progression: Repeat the sequence standing and add a short walking break.
recipes.cautions: Seek medical guidance for recent trauma, severe headache, dizziness, faintness, numbness, or progressive weakness.

recipes.title: Ribcage breathing reset
recipes.goal: Practice quieter breathing with coordinated rib and abdominal movement
recipes.whenToUse: Breathing feels upper-chest dominant during low-intensity movement or recovery work.
recipes.steps:
1. Choose a comfortable supported position.
2. Inhale gently through the nose without forcing a large breath.
3. Exhale slowly and allow the lower ribs to settle.
4. Add a relaxed arm reach while maintaining the same breathing rhythm.
recipes.dosage: Complete 2 rounds of 4–5 slow breaths. Rest normally between rounds.
recipes.reassess: Check whether the neck and upper chest feel less involved in each breath.
recipes.regression: Remove the arm reach and use a more upright supported position.
recipes.progression: Maintain the same breathing pattern during an easy sit-to-stand or walk.
recipes.cautions: Stop if breathing becomes difficult, you feel faint, or you develop chest pain. Seek urgent care for severe breathing symptoms.
recipes.sourceName: Cambridge University Hospitals Breathing Pattern Guidance

recipes.title: Pelvic balance baseline
recipes.goal: Build awareness and control around the pelvis before harder lower-body work
recipes.whenToUse: Weight shifts or single-leg tasks feel uneven without sharp pain or recent injury.
recipes.steps:
1. Stand with light hand support.
2. Shift weight slowly from side to side without collapsing the trunk.
3. Hold a comfortable single-leg position for a few seconds.
4. Practice a controlled step-back and return.
5. Reassess side-to-side confidence.
recipes.dosage: Use 2 rounds of 5 weight shifts, 3 short holds per side, and 5 step-backs.
recipes.reassess: Compare steadiness, foot pressure, and trunk control between sides.
recipes.regression: Keep both feet down and use more hand support.
recipes.progression: Reduce hand support or add a longer pause while keeping the pelvis level.
recipes.cautions: Stop if the hip catches, gives way, or produces sharp groin pain.

recipes.title: Knee control before squatting
recipes.goal: Practice comfortable knee tracking and controlled loading before deeper squats
recipes.whenToUse: A shallow squat or stair pattern feels hesitant but walking is comfortable and the knee is not swollen.
recipes.steps:
1. Practice a supported sit-to-stand with even foot pressure.
2. Add a slow step-down from a very low height or a controlled knee bend.
3. Keep the knee tracking in line with the middle toes.
4. Reassess a shallow squat.
recipes.dosage: Perform 2 rounds of 5 sit-to-stands and 4–6 controlled knee bends per side.
recipes.reassess: Check comfort, confidence, knee tracking, and control on the way down.
recipes.regression: Use a higher chair and more hand support.
recipes.progression: Lower the chair slightly or slow the lowering phase.
recipes.cautions: Stop for increasing swelling, locking, giving way, sharp pain, or inability to bear weight.

recipes.title: Ankle rehabilitation progression
recipes.goal: Rebuild comfortable ankle motion, balance, strength, and confidence after an ankle sprain
recipes.whenToUse: The acute stage has settled, weight bearing is tolerated, and rehabilitation exercise has been cleared.
recipes.steps:
1. Begin only after the acute stage has settled and exercise has been cleared.
2. Restore comfortable ankle motion without forcing symptoms.
3. Rebuild balance and controlled weight bearing.
4. Progress calf and ankle strength gradually.
5. Reassess walking and task tolerance before advancing.
recipes.dosage: Use 2 rounds of 8–12 mobility or strength repetitions and 3 balance holds of 10–20 seconds.
recipes.reassess: Compare swelling response, walking comfort, balance, and confidence later the same day and the next morning.
recipes.regression: Use two-leg support, shorten the balance hold, and reduce resistance.
recipes.progression: Increase range, resistance, or single-leg demand one variable at a time.
recipes.cautions: Stop and seek clinical guidance if pain or swelling increases, the ankle gives way, walking remains difficult, or the calf becomes hot and swollen.
recipes.sourceName: AAOS Foot and Ankle Conditioning Program

recipes.title: Foot tripod walking reset
recipes.goal: Improve awareness of heel, big-toe, and little-toe pressure during standing and walking
recipes.whenToUse: The foot feels unstable or disconnected during easy standing and walking without acute injury.
recipes.steps:
1. Stand with light support and feel three points of contact under each foot.
2. Shift weight forward and backward without gripping the toes.
3. Practice a slow calf raise while maintaining even pressure.
4. Walk slowly for several steps and reassess foot contact.
recipes.dosage: Use 2 rounds of 5 weight shifts, 6 calf raises, and 10–20 slow walking steps.
recipes.reassess: Check whether foot pressure feels more even and walking feels steadier.
recipes.regression: Keep both hands supported and reduce the calf-raise height.
recipes.progression: Use less hand support or add a short single-leg balance hold.
recipes.cautions: Stop for sharp foot pain, new numbness, increasing swelling, or inability to bear weight comfortably.
recipes.relatedConditions: Foot control, walking mechanics, ankle stability
recipes.sourceName: AAOS Foot and Ankle Conditioning Program

recipes.title: Overhead reach preparation
recipes.goal: Prepare the shoulder blade and rotator cuff for a smoother unloaded overhead reach
recipes.whenToUse: Reaching overhead feels effortful or coordinated poorly, but there is no acute injury, marked weakness, or resting pain.
recipes.steps:
1. Warm up with easy walking or arm swings for several minutes.
2. Practice a small wall slide while keeping the neck relaxed.
3. Add a light band external-rotation hold with the elbow near the side.
4. Repeat the wall slide through a comfortable range.
5. Reassess one unloaded overhead reach.
recipes.dosage: Perform 2 rounds of 5 wall slides and 5 light rotation holds of 5 seconds per side.
recipes.reassess: Compare comfort, range, shoulder-blade movement, and neck effort with the first reach.
recipes.regression: Shorten the wall-slide range and remove band resistance.
recipes.progression: Increase the reach slightly or use a very light band only when every repetition stays pain-free and controlled.
recipes.cautions: Stop for pain, new weakness, numbness, instability, or symptoms traveling down the arm. Seek individual guidance if you are unsure which exercise is appropriate.
recipes.relatedConditions: Overhead reach, scapular control, shoulder external rotation
recipes.sourceName: AAOS Rotator Cuff and Shoulder Conditioning Program

recipes.title: Thoracic rotation reset
recipes.goal: Explore comfortable upper-trunk rotation without forcing the lower back or neck
recipes.whenToUse: Turning through the upper trunk feels stiff after prolonged sitting and gentle movement normally feels helpful.
recipes.steps:
1. Sit with both feet supported and take three relaxed breaths.
2. Cross the arms lightly over the chest.
3. Turn the upper trunk a small comfortable amount while keeping the pelvis quiet.
4. Exhale gently, return to center, and repeat on the other side.
5. Reassess an easy seated turn.
recipes.dosage: Use 2 rounds of 4–6 slow turns per side without pushing into pain.
recipes.reassess: Compare side-to-side range, effort, and whether breathing remains relaxed.
recipes.regression: Use a smaller range and keep the hands supported on the thighs.
recipes.progression: Repeat standing with the hips still, or carry the improved rotation into an easy walk.
recipes.cautions: Stop if pain increases or spreads into the arm or leg, or if you feel numbness, weakness, dizziness, or unwell.
recipes.relatedConditions: Thoracic rotation, prolonged sitting, breathing coordination

recipes.title: Trunk control before lifting
recipes.goal: Coordinate breathing, hip movement, and trunk control before light lifting practice
recipes.whenToUse: A hip hinge feels unfamiliar or the lower back does most of the work during easy daily lifting.
recipes.steps:
1. Take three relaxed breaths in standing.
2. Practice sending the hips back toward a wall while keeping the object close to the body.
3. Return to standing by pressing through the feet.
4. Add a very light object only if the unloaded hinge feels comfortable.
5. Reassess the unloaded hinge after the set.
recipes.dosage: Complete 2 rounds of 5–8 slow hinges, resting between rounds.
recipes.reassess: Check whether the movement feels more evenly shared between the hips, legs, and trunk.
recipes.regression: Move the wall closer and practice without an object.
recipes.progression: Move slightly farther from the wall or add a light object while keeping the same control.
recipes.cautions: Stop if back pain worsens, symptoms travel into the leg, or numbness, weakness, bowel or bladder changes, or feeling unwell occurs.
recipes.relatedConditions: Hip hinge, trunk control, lifting preparation

recipes.title: Hip control walking preparation
recipes.goal: Wake up lateral-hip control before walking or lower-body training
recipes.whenToUse: The pelvis shifts noticeably during easy single-leg support but walking remains comfortable.
recipes.steps:
1. Warm up with several minutes of easy walking.
2. Stand beside a stable support and shift weight onto one leg.
3. Lift the opposite foot slightly without leaning the trunk.
4. Add a small side step while keeping the feet facing forward.
5. Walk ten easy steps and reassess steadiness.
recipes.dosage: Use 2 rounds of 5 controlled weight shifts and 5 small side steps per direction.
recipes.reassess: Compare pelvic steadiness, foot pressure, and walking confidence between sides.
recipes.regression: Keep both feet on the floor and use more hand support.
recipes.progression: Use less support or add a longer single-leg pause before each side step.
recipes.cautions: Stop for sharp groin pain, catching, giving way, or increasing pain during or after the sequence.
recipes.relatedConditions: Hip abductor control, pelvic balance, walking asymmetry

recipes.title: Stair control preparation
recipes.goal: Practice controlled knee loading before repeated stair use
recipes.whenToUse: Stairs feel hesitant but level walking is comfortable and the knee is not acutely swollen or unstable.
recipes.equipment: Bottom stair or low step, handrail
recipes.steps:
1. Warm up with several minutes of easy walking.
2. Practice a supported sit-to-stand from a comfortable height.
3. Place one foot on a low step and shift weight forward without pushing into pain.
4. Practice a slow step-up with handrail support.
5. Reassess one normal stair step.
recipes.dosage: Perform 2 rounds of 5 sit-to-stands and 4–6 supported step-ups per side.
recipes.reassess: Compare confidence, knee tracking, and control during the lowering phase.
recipes.regression: Use a lower step, more hand support, or repeat only the forward weight shift.
recipes.progression: Reduce hand support or slow the lowering phase before increasing step height.
recipes.cautions: Stop if the knee swells, locks, gives way, or produces pain that persists after stopping.
recipes.relatedConditions: Stair control, knee extensor strength, lower-limb alignment

recipes.title: Knee extension baseline
recipes.goal: Practice comfortable quadriceps control before harder standing tasks
recipes.whenToUse: The thigh feels difficult to engage during easy straightening, without a recent injury or substantial swelling.
recipes.steps:
1. Warm up with easy walking or cycling if available.
2. Sit or lie with a rolled towel supporting the knee.
3. Gently straighten the knee and tighten the front of the thigh.
4. Pause briefly, then lower with control.
5. Reassess a supported sit-to-stand.
recipes.dosage: Perform 2 rounds of 6–10 comfortable repetitions with a brief pause at the top.
recipes.reassess: Check whether the knee straightens more confidently and the sit-to-stand feels steadier.
recipes.regression: Use a smaller straightening range and a shorter pause.
recipes.progression: Add repetitions gradually before adding resistance or a harder standing task.
recipes.cautions: Stop if exercise causes pain, increasing swelling, locking, giving way, or difficulty moving afterward.

recipes.title: Calf raise readiness
recipes.goal: Prepare the calf and ankle for controlled push-off during walking
recipes.whenToUse: Walking is comfortable but push-off feels weak or uneven, without acute injury or increasing swelling.
recipes.steps:
1. Warm up with several minutes of easy walking.
2. Practice ankle motion while seated.
3. Stand with both hands supported and rise onto both forefeet slowly.
4. Lower under control while keeping pressure through the big-toe and little-toe sides.
5. Walk ten easy steps and reassess push-off.
recipes.dosage: Use 2 rounds of 6–10 two-leg calf raises with a comfortable rest between rounds.
recipes.reassess: Compare heel-rise height, control, foot pressure, and walking symmetry.
recipes.regression: Use more arm support, reduce height, or practice seated ankle movement only.
recipes.progression: Reduce hand support or shift slightly more weight to one side before attempting single-leg work.
recipes.cautions: Stop for sharp pain, increasing swelling, inability to bear weight, or a hot and swollen calf. Seek urgent assessment for sudden calf symptoms.
recipes.relatedConditions: Calf strength, ankle push-off, walking mechanics
recipes.sourceName: AAOS Foot and Ankle Conditioning Program
